forces: Soprano, alto, mixed chorus and orchestra
intro: Mahler’s resurrection begins with an orchestral cry and reaches the human voice only after marches, distant brass and birdsong. The chorus’s first answer is almost a whisper; its last brings organ, bells and the whole orchestra into E♭ major.

cues.title: The cry returns
cues.text: The scherzo’s orchestral outcry bursts into the silence after Urlicht. Then the horns offer a hesitant phrase that will become the resurrection theme. The melody is here long before anyone can sing its words.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 2, Hofmeister full score (1897), movement V, opening; the recalled cry and horn theme are described at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-5-lied-2-auferstehung-im-tempo-des-scherzos/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Calls across an empty space
cues.text: Horn calls sound from beyond the orchestra. Descending triplets travel down through the winds; a measured wind chorale walks over plucked string quavers. Pauses separate these little scenes, each with its own instruments and its own distance.
cues.evidence: The offstage horns, descending triplets and wind chorale over pizzicato quavers belong to the orchestral prelude: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-5-lied-2-auferstehung-im-tempo-des-scherzos/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A chorale from the Dies irae
cues.text: Out of silence, woodwinds play a quiet chorale over plucked strings. It echoes the Dies irae from the first movement’s funeral march, and some of its intervals already belong to the resurrection theme.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 142 (Langsam, quasi l’istesso Tempo): flute, oboe and clarinet play the chorale pianissimo over pizzicato violas and cellos, with four flats in the signature. The Mahler Foundation’s page on the movement describes a wind chorale against pizzicato quavers that recalls the first movement’s Dies irae and announces intervals of the resurrection theme: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-5-lied-2-auferstehung-im-tempo-des-scherzos/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A hymn at Bülow’s funeral
cues.text: Hamburg, 29 March 1894. At Hans von Bülow’s memorial service, Mahler hears Klopstock’s resurrection hymn. It supplies the words he has been searching for; he takes its first two stanzas and writes the rest of the finale’s text himself.
cues.evidence: Memorial service and hymn: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-history/ . Klopstock’s first two stanzas and Mahler’s continuation are printed in the full score.

cues.title: A trombone, then a trumpet
cues.text: A solo trombone, marked bestimmt — decisively — takes the chorale up, and a trumpet follows. Horns then come to the front, offstage horns call again, and the strings tremble away to nothing.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 142, rehearsal 5: first trombone p bestimmt, then first trumpet, over pizzicato strings. P. 143, rehearsal 6 (Nicht eilen): horns marked sehr hervortretend, a group of horns in the distance (stark geblasen), and divided string tremolo marked verhallend, dying away.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cries of woe peak in a shriek
cues.text: Cries pass between the winds and quicken: Mahler asks for Etwas drängend, somewhat pressing, then Sehr drängend, very pressing, and the woodwinds rise to fortissimo. Then the sound drains away into the low trombones and a faint timpani roll.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 145 (rehearsal 7, Etwas drängend), p. 146 (rehearsal 8, Sehr drängend, with flutes, oboes, cor anglais, clarinets and bassoons at ff) and p. 147 (Wieder zurückhaltend: low trombones and a timpani roll fading to ppp).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The low brass alone
cues.text: After a general pause the trombones and tuba, with the contrabassoon, sing a broad chorale, Wieder sehr breit. Trumpets join, and a long crescendo drives the music towards a brass fanfare.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 148, rehearsal 10: G.P., then Wieder sehr breit for contrabassoon, trombones and tuba with five flats in the signature; Etwas energischer im Tempo brings in the trumpets under a long crescendo, with a conductor’s note on the crescendo. The Mahler Foundation’s page describes a reply in the form of a chorale to which the lower brass add solemnity, followed by the return of the brass fanfare: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-5-lied-2-auferstehung-im-tempo-des-scherzos/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The fanfare returns in C major
cues.text: The brass fanfare comes back in C major. Horns and trumpets trade volleys of repeated calls over harps and cymbals, while running figures churn in the winds and strings. The resurrection theme sounds again, far more assertive than before.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 149–151: rehearsal 11 (Wieder breit, no sharps or flats in the signature), horn and trumpet volleys with harp glissandos and cymbals on p. 150, woodwind and string runs from rehearsal 12 on p. 151. The Mahler Foundation’s page says the return of the brass fanfare prepares a new statement of the resurrection theme, now far more assertive: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-5-lied-2-auferstehung-im-tempo-des-scherzos/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The drums start a march
cues.text: A percussion crescendo leads to a brass fanfare and the Allegro energico. Earlier tunes now march, with sharply bitten rhythms and fast string figures. Mahler adds Nicht zu schnell: energetic, but not too fast.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 154–155: percussion crescendo, Maestoso fanfare, Allegro energico, Nicht zu schnell and Sehr scharf rhythmisiert.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The Dies irae marches
cues.text: The Dies irae turns into a march, serious and at first upbeat, and the trumpets lay a solemn, chorale-like variation of the same melody over it. At Kräftig, vigorously, Mahler notes that a brisk march tempo has now been reached.
cues.evidence: Bettie Jo Basinger, Utah Symphony listening guide: the Dies irae becomes a serious, initially upbeat march, with a trumpet chorale-like variation of the same melody above it: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide . Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 158: Kräftig, with the note that a fresh march tempo has been reached in the course of the pressing movement (Hier ist im Verlaufe des drängenden Satzes ein frisches Marschtempo erreicht worden).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bells against the march
cues.text: Deep bells of no fixed pitch ring out against the march, and the woodwinds raise their bells just before. Mahler writes for three such bells, in three passages of the movement that add up to twenty-two bars.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 160 (rehearsal 16: Schalltrichter auf in the woodwinds) and p. 161 (Wieder etwas gehaltener; a staff for 3 Stahlstäbe oder Glocken von tiefem und unbestimmtem Klange); further bell staves in the coda, pp. 206–209. The Mahler Foundation’s page lists three low bells in three passages of the movement, 22 bars in total: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-5-lied-2-auferstehung-im-tempo-des-scherzos/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Written in three weeks, signed in December
cues.text: Mahler jots down sketches for the finale as soon as he reaches home from Bülow’s funeral, and completes it within about three weeks the following summer. The autograph full score of the whole symphony is signed on 18 December 1894.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation introduction gives the immediate sketches and the three weeks of composition: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-introduction/ . Its history page dates the autograph full score to 18 December 1894: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-history/

cues.title: Cellos against distant trumpets
cues.text: The march breaks down into speech-like string phrases. Cellos and bassoons sing in the foreground while distant trumpets and percussion continue behind them. Mahler tells the conductor to keep those far-off fanfares from disturbing the melody.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 174–176, especially rehearsal 22 on p. 175 and its direction about balancing the distant instruments against cellos and bassoons.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The plea behind “O glaube”
cues.text: The cellos’ pleading phrases, in shifting duple and triple metres, are the “O glaube” material. Much later the alto will sing “O glaube, mein Herz” — believe, my heart — to a return of the same pleading phrases.
cues.evidence: Bettie Jo Basinger, Utah Symphony listening guide: the development resumes with the “O glaube” material, and Mahler later sets the text to these pleading phrases: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide . Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 174 (cellos molto espress. after the solo trombone) and p. 175, rehearsal 22 (Mit etwas drängendem Charakter): cellos and first bassoon in changing 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 bars.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A band in the distance
cues.text: Far off, a band of trumpets, triangle, cymbals and bass drum plays fanfare signals that cut across the cellos’ pleading again and again. Mahler sets the band at the greatest distance and, at one point, asks for it to sound much stronger. It is an early example of music placed in space.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 175 (rehearsal 22) and pp. 176–179 (rehearsals 23–25): trumpets in F and in C, several players each, with triangle, cymbals and bass drum, marked in weitester Ferne aufgestellt; p. 178 carries the direction Hier soll die Musik viel stärker hörbar sein. The Mahler Foundation’s page describes offstage brass superimposing fanfare motifs on the recitative as one of the earliest instances of a spatialization effect: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-5-lied-2-auferstehung-im-tempo-des-scherzos/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The graves burst open
cues.text: The orchestra drives to its climax. Mahler marks Più mosso and molto accelerando, and winds, horns and trumpets blare fortissimo over a welter of percussion: triangle, bass drum, cymbals, tam-tam and timpani. Mahler’s own programme: “The earth trembles, the graves burst open, the dead arise and march forth in endless procession.”
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 181–182 (rehearsal 26: Più mosso, molto accelerando, Ganze Takte schlagen, Poco rit.; woodwind, horn and trumpet staves at ff to fff, with triangle, bass drum, cymbals, tam-tam and timpani). Bettie Jo Basinger, Utah Symphony listening guide: the tempo accelerates, the volume rises and the dissonance increases before horn fanfares surface from the din: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide . The programme text, in the Foundation’s translation: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-introduction/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The hush after the climax
cues.text: The climax collapses into a hush. Mahler marks Langsam, holding back more and more. Horns sound soft chords, a timpani roll murmurs underneath, and an oboe and cellos sing quiet, separate lines while the clarinets answer like an echo.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 183, rehearsal 27: Langsam, immer noch mehr zurückhaltend; five flats in the signature; pp horn chords in three pairs, timpani tremolo sempre pp, glockenspiel, oboe and cello lines, and the clarinets marked (Echo).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Brass calls, birds answer
cues.text: The great summons leaves the main orchestra almost empty. Trumpets call from opposing directions; horns hold distant notes. Flute and piccolo answer with birdsong. There are long spaces in which only one small sound remains.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 185–186: spatial directions for trumpets, distant horns, and flute and piccolo marked wie eine Vogelstimme.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Berlin, 13 December 1895
cues.text: Mahler conducts the first complete performance of the symphony in Berlin on 13 December 1895. Nine months earlier the city had heard only the first three movements. The audience applauds warmly; the next morning’s newspapers renew the attacks.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation introduction describes the enthusiastic response and the bitter notices the next morning: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-introduction/ . Its history page dates the first three movements to 4 March 1895 and the complete première to 13 December 1895: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-history/

cues.title: Mahler’s nightingale
cues.text: In Mahler’s programme the last trumpet sounds, and in the eerie silence that follows we hear “a distant nightingale, a last tremulous echo of earthly life”. The flute and piccolo, marked like a bird’s voice, answer that image.
cues.evidence: Programme text in the Mahler Foundation introduction: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-introduction/ . Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide links the nightingale to the flute marked wie eine Vogelstimme: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide

cues.title: The chorus begins softly
cues.text: The chorus begins in G♭ major, unaccompanied and almost inaudible. Klopstock’s hymn promises that dust will rise again after a short rest. The soprano soloist sings within the choral sound; Mahler asks her to avoid standing out.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 186, rehearsal 31: Langsam. Misterioso, chorus a cappella at ppp, soprano ohne im Geringsten hervorzutreten. The opening text is Klopstock’s.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mahler alters Klopstock
cues.text: Klopstock wrote that the one who made you (“der dich schuf”) will give you immortal life. Mahler sets “der dich rief”: the one who called you. He also turns “I shall be sown” into “you will be sown”, and drops the Hallelujahs.
cues.evidence: Paul Banks’s Mahler catalogue prints Klopstock’s text (Wird, der dich schuf; werd ich gesät; Halleluja) beside Mahler’s version (der dich rief; wirst du gesät): https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/Symph2/Texts.htm

cues.title: The orchestra takes the hymn
cues.text: The chorus completes its first stanza, the soprano soloist singing within its line, and the orchestra takes over alone. Mahler marks Sehr breit, very broad, for horns and trumpets in portamento, then Streng im Tempo, strictly in time, with long bows in the strings. The chorus returns for the second stanza.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 187 (rehearsal 32: “Unsterblich Leben wird, der dich rief, dir geben”, with the soprano soloist among the choral staves; rehearsal 33: Sehr breit, horns and trumpets molto portamento) and pp. 188–189 (rehearsal 34: Streng im Tempo, first and second violins lang gezogen, viel Bogen). Bettie Jo Basinger, Utah Symphony listening guide: an orchestral interlude follows the first stanza, and the chorus interrupts it to deliver the second: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The lord of the harvest
cues.text: Klopstock’s second stanza turns to the fields: “To bloom again you are sown! The Lord of the harvest goes and gathers in, like sheaves, us who died.” The chorus sings it quietly. The orchestra then closes Klopstock’s text on its own before Mahler’s words begin.
cues.evidence: Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide prints Klopstock’s stanzas and Mahler’s continuation in German and English, and describes the second stanza and the orchestral interlude that ends Klopstock’s text: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide . Translation by the site.

cues.title: A MiniDisc in Wheaton
cues.text: This is Barbara Schubert’s DuPage Symphony Orchestra in Edman Memorial Chapel, Wheaton College, Illinois, on 22 May 2004. Eric Pancer taped the concert on a Sony MiniDisc recorder and put it on the Internet Archive that December.
cues.evidence: Internet Archive item metadata for “Resurrection!” (taper, equipment, venue, concert date and upload dates): https://archive.org/details/dupageso-2004-05-22

cues.title: The alto’s private appeal
cues.text: Mahler’s own words begin with an appeal to the heart. The alto sings in B♭ minor beside a cor anglais, over muted strings and plucked bass notes. The huge public hymn contracts to two dark, intimate voices.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 193, rehearsal 39: O glaube, mein Herz, o glaube, alto with cor anglais, muted divided strings and pizzicato basses.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The soprano takes up the plea
cues.text: The soprano answers the alto: “O believe, you were not born in vain!” A solo violin carries her line further, the strings tremble beneath it, and a harp glissando sweeps upward into the next section.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 194 (rehearsal 41: soprano solo “O glaube: Du wardst nicht umsonst geboren!”) and p. 195 (soprano continuing; first violin Solo on the D string; harp glissando at rehearsal 42 with the instruction that its first note be strongly accented). The soprano’s line follows the alto’s in Mahler’s text, printed in German in Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide . Translation by the site.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Stop trembling, prepare to live
cues.text: Low voices bring back the resurrection theme with Mahler’s own words, “Was entstanden ist, das muss vergehen”, over trombones and tuba and a high violin trill. The chorus calls out “auferstehen”, then alto and chorus whisper “Hör’ auf zu beben!” — stop trembling — before the voices urge “Bereite dich zu leben!” — prepare to live.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 195 (rehearsal 42, Langsamer. Misterioso: alto, tenor and bass sing “Was entstanden ist, das muss vergehen”, with trombones and tuba and violin trills), p. 196 (rehearsal 43: “auferstehen”, then “Hör’ auf zu beben” at ppp with the alto soloist marked ohne hervorzutreten, then “Bereite dich zu leben”, Schneller) and p. 197. Bettie Jo Basinger, Utah Symphony listening guide: the chorus returns with the Auferstehen material, now singing Mahler’s text: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two voices answer pain and death
cues.text: Alto and soprano sing “O Schmerz! Du Alldurchdringer!” — O pain, you all-penetrating. Mahler marks the passage Mit Aufschwung, aber nicht eilen, with uplift, but not hurrying, and later Vorwärts and Drängend press the duet on. It briefly recalls the melody of Urlicht.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 197 (rehearsal 44: Mit Aufschwung, aber nicht eilen; “O Schmerz! Du Alldurchdringer!”), p. 198 (rehearsal 45: “O Tod! Du Allbezwinger!”) and p. 199 (Vorwärts, Drängend, Nicht schleppen: “Mit Flügeln … werd’ ich entschweben”). Bettie Jo Basinger, Utah Symphony listening guide: the passage marked Mit Aufschwung, and the duet’s reference to the Urlicht melody: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The whisper becomes a proclamation
cues.text: The first choral melody returns in E♭ major with brass and organ. Soprano and alto join the chorus; the organ is marked volles Werk, full organ. The tune that began without accompaniment now has the whole building behind it.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 204, rehearsal 48: Aufersteh’n return, soloists with chorus, brass and organ marked volles Werk.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mahler on the final climax
cues.text: Mahler tells Natalie Bauer-Lechner that the build-up and surge of the closing pages are “so immense that afterwards even I do not know how I came to write it”.
cues.evidence: Natalie Bauer-Lechner, Erinnerungen an Gustav Mahler (Leipzig: E. P. Tal, 1923), pp. 23–24, in the section “Deutung der Zweiten Symphonie”: “Die Steigerung und der Aufschwung, der jetzt bis zum Schlusse folgt, ist ein so ungeheurer, daß ich selbst hinterher nicht weiß, wie ich dazu gelangen konnte.” Translation ours. https://archive.org/details/erinnerungengust00baue . The Mahler Foundation’s page on the Collier bell foundry quotes the same remark in English: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/locations/germany/berlin/city-of-berlin//bell-foundry-collier/

cues.title: Mahler goes hunting for bells
cues.text: On 8 December 1895, five days before the première, Mahler writes to the soprano Anna von Mildenburg about the bells he needs. He has taken the train to a foundry at Zehlendorf, through snowy firs, because “only a bell founder could help me”.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation quotes Mahler’s letter of 8 December 1895 to Anna Bahr-von Mildenburg about his visit to the Collier foundry: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/locations/germany/berlin/city-of-berlin//bell-foundry-collier/

cues.title: Bells after the voices
cues.text: The singers finish and the orchestra carries on, with organ and bells sounding through E♭ major. On the last page Mahler asks for the utmost force, then a sharply cut-off ending. The final chord is released together.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 206–209; p. 209 gives Mit höchster Kraftentfaltung and scharf abgerissen.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Trumpets over the closing chord
cues.text: Over a sustained E♭ major chord the trumpets sound a short two-note figure again and again, loud and then louder. The long closing chord is sounded by all ten horns among the full orchestra, with organ and bells.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 208–209: horn staves for players 1 to 10, trumpets repeating a two-note figure marked ff and then fff over Noch einmal so langsam, organ volles Werk, a bell staff and tam-tam, and scharf abreissen on the last bar. Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide gives the movement ten horns, four of them offstage earlier: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Horn calls emerge from the outburst
transitions.to: A · Horn calls and wind chorales
transitions.how: The opening orchestral cry recedes into horn phrases and pauses. Offstage horns answer, and descending triplets travel down through the winds. The prelude then sets a wind chorale over pizzicato string quavers.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 134–145; prelude described at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-5-lied-2-auferstehung-im-tempo-des-scherzos/

transitions.title: Percussion lifts the brass fanfare
transitions.from: A · Horn calls and wind chorales
transitions.how: Percussion grows out of the retreating prelude into a Maestoso brass fanfare. The following Allegro energico puts running strings beneath sharply accented march figures. Mahler writes Nicht zu schnell, keeping the beat firm under the quick notes.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister full score (1897), movement V, pp. 154–155.

transitions.title: The cellos begin to speak
transitions.to: Link · Cellos speak against distant trumpets
transitions.how: The march breaks off and the cellos take up irregular, recitative-like phrases. Bassoons join them above restrained strings. Distant trumpet and percussion calls continue separately; the score explicitly protects the cello and bassoon melody from their interruption.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 174–176, rehearsal 22 and its balance instruction.

transitions.title: The brass moves into the distance
transitions.from: Link · Cellos speak against distant trumpets
transitions.how: The strings withdraw. Horns and trumpets call across long holds and pauses, with the trumpets directed to sound from opposite sides. Flute and piccolo supply the nearby birdsong, small quick figures between the brass notes.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 183–186, especially the spatial directions on p. 185.

transitions.title: G♭ major, without the orchestra
transitions.to: C · The chorus whispers of resurrection
transitions.how: The distant calls and birdsong disappear. At Langsam. Misterioso the chorus begins in G♭ major, a cappella and ppp. The soprano soloist blends into the upper choral line, while the bass voices supply the foundation the orchestra has left empty.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 186, rehearsal 31.

transitions.title: Alto and cor anglais in B♭ minor
transitions.from: C · The chorus whispers of resurrection
transitions.to: D · The alto addresses the heart
transitions.how: After the choral stanzas and orchestral replies, the alto begins in B♭ minor. A cor anglais winds around the vocal line; muted divided strings and pizzicato basses leave room for both. The soprano takes up the appeal afterwards.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 193–194, rehearsal 39 onwards.

transitions.title: The chorus answers the soloists
transitions.from: D · The alto addresses the heart
transitions.to: Dev · Chorus and soloists confront death
transitions.how: The soprano’s phrase slows and the strings retreat. A harp glissando leads towards the lower choral voices; trumpets, trombones and tuba answer their measured phrases. Mahler marks the passage Langsamer. Misterioso before the soloists’ duet begins its climb.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, p. 195, rehearsal 42, and the subsequent duet.

transitions.title: Organ joins the E♭-major chorus
transitions.from: Dev · Chorus and soloists confront death
transitions.to: C′ · Resurrection with organ and brass
transitions.how: Overlapping choral lines climb through a crescendo. The resurrection melody returns in E♭ major, marked Pesante, with the soloists joining the chorus. Full organ and broad brass chords stand beneath the voices, sustaining the harmony through their long phrases.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 202–204, reaching rehearsal 48 with organ marked volles Werk.

transitions.title: The bells outlast the words
transitions.from: C′ · Resurrection with organ and brass
transitions.to: Coda · Bells and the final E♭
transitions.how: The voices finish while the instruments continue in E♭ major. Brass, strings and organ sustain the closing harmony, and bells sound above the bass. The final page broadens to half speed before the orchestra cuts off the last chord together.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement V, pp. 206–209; Noch einmal so langsam and scharf abgerissen on the final page.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 2, full score (Hofmeister 1897; Weinberger/Universal Edition reprint)
source.locator: Finale, pp. 134–209: orchestral prelude and march, distant calls, a cappella chorus, soprano and alto solos, and the E♭-major ending with organ and bells.

timeline.note: Brass and strings launch the opening outburst; voices and organ wait.
Separated horn calls and wind phrases emerge from the opening outburst.
Wind chorales and descending figures alternate above moving and plucked strings.
A percussion crescendo leads into brass fanfares and a march with running strings.
Cellos and bassoons sing against distant trumpets and percussion; the other strings hold back.
Distant horns, trumpets and percussion answer the nearby flute and piccolo birdsong.
The chorus begins without accompaniment; the soprano soloist blends into its sound.
Winds, brass and strings answer the chorus’s first stanza.
Quiet voices begin the second Klopstock stanza; strings enter around their phrases.
Alto and cor anglais sing over muted strings; the soprano takes up the appeal afterwards.
Soprano and alto address pain and death, with strings, harp and soft wind and brass phrases.
Chorus and soloists sing the resurrection theme with brass, strings and full organ.
Organ, bells and orchestra complete the E♭-major ending after the voices finish.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
